findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, colliding anonymous and render subjects
findings.body: The permission-denial cache is keyed by userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent), where UserUID is the raw identifier parsed from the subject. Both the anonymous identity ("anonymous:0") and the render service ("render:0") parse to the identifier "0", and the denial cache is consulted in Check() before any identity-type-specific logic. So a denial recorded for an anonymous Check (denials are cached for anonymous users via the normal path) will short-circuit a subsequent render-service Check for the same action/resource/folder and return Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions() unconditionally grants read access to all dashboards/folders. The reverse contamination is also possible: the render service gets an empty permission map for non-read actions, and those denials are cached under "0", which then blocks anonymous checks that should have gone to the database. The consequence is broken dashboard rendering and incorrect denials whenever these two identity types share the "0" identifier. The key should include the identity type (and the resolved user UID).

findings.title: Denial cache is never invalidated and bypasses the new DB-requery fallback
findings.body: Check() consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns deny immediately on a hit, and the entry is only written after a database query returns deny, with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) and no invalidation path anywhere in the service. This undermines the PR's own fix: when cached permissions lack a resource, Check now re-queries the database so that newly granted permissions take effect — but if the (user, action, name, parent) combination was denied within the last 30 seconds, the denial entry short-circuits before the requery, so a permission grant on a previously denied resource is not visible for up to the full TTL. In the remote/cloud deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the injected cache may be shared across instances, so the stale denial applies fleet-wide. There is no Delete/invalidate call for permDenialCache on permission changes, so any grant/revocation asymmetry is purely time-bounded. Maintainers should either invalidate denial entries when permissions change or exclude recently-denied entries when a fresh DB query is the intended source of truth.

findings.title: Denial cache key uses ambiguous '_' delimiters with unescaped components
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent, where name (resource UID) and parent (folder UID) are caller-supplied and user-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores. Two different requests can therefore produce identical keys, e.g. name="x", parent="y_z" and name="x_y", parent="z" both yield "..._x_y_z". A denial cached for one resource/folder pair would then incorrectly deny a different resource for up to 30 seconds. Since the values are arbitrary identifiers, the key components should be escaped or a non-ambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or hashed) should be used.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits and perm-cache misses with existing semantics
findings.body: On a denial-cache hit, Check() increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true", making denial-cache hits indistinguishable from permission-map cache hits in dashboards/alerts. Additionally, when the permission map is found in cache but the specific resource is absent (cache hit, deny), the code falls through and increments permissionCacheUsage with "false", so a genuine cache hit is now recorded as a miss. Existing monitors built on this metric's previous meaning (hit = allowed-from-cache) will silently change behavior after this PR; a separate label or metric for the new denial cache would preserve the contract.

findings.title: "should return error if store fails" test never triggers an error
findings.body: In TestService_getUserPermissions, the case named "should return error if store fails" sets permissions to nil but the fakeStore constructed in the loop never sets err: true, and the test then calls require.NoError(t, err). It therefore exercises the empty-permission success path rather than the error path it claims to cover, giving false confidence that store failures are handled. Relatedly, after this PR removed the cache-hit case, the testCase.cacheHit field and the "if tc.cacheHit" assertion branch (including the "only get user id" expectation) are dead code that no test can reach; either restore a cache-hit case at the new getCachedIdentityPermissions level or remove the field.
